\section[\texorpdfstring{\kn{ಕಮಲ} (kamala)}{ಕಮಲ (kamala)}]{\kn{ಕಮಲ} (kamala) — a lotus}

\label{lesson:KA-C139-kamala}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Kannada for socks, then the Kannada for a coat.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಕಮಲ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಕಮಲ}} — \emph{kamala} — \textquotedblleft{}a lotus\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಕಮಲ}} (\emph{kamala}) is Sanskrit \emph{kamala}, \textquotedblleft{}lotus\textquotedblright{}, taken over whole as a learned loan, a tatsama (CDIAL 2764). CDIAL, following Mayrhofer, takes the Sanskrit word itself to be a loan from Dravidian.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kamala}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{kamala}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Kannada for socks, then the Kannada for a coat, then say \emph{kamala} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\kn{ಗೋಧಿ} (gōdhi)}{ಗೋಧಿ (gōdhi)}]{\kn{ಗೋಧಿ} (gōdhi) — wheat}

\label{lesson:KA-C139-godhi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Kannada for a coat, then the Kannada for a lotus.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಗೋಧಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಗೋಧಿ}} — \emph{gōdhi} — \textquotedblleft{}wheat\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಗೋಧಿ}} (\emph{gōdhi}) is usually traced to Sanskrit \emph{godhūma}, \textquotedblleft{}wheat\textquotedblright{}: a tadbhava, a loan worn down in speech.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\kn{ದೋಣಿ} (dōṇi)}{ದೋಣಿ (dōṇi)}]{\kn{ದೋಣಿ} (dōṇi) — a boat}

\label{lesson:KA-C139-doni}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Kannada for a lotus, then the Kannada for wheat.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ದೋಣಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ದೋಣಿ}} — \emph{dōṇi} — \textquotedblleft{}a boat\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ದೋಣಿ}} (\emph{dōṇi}) comes from Sanskrit \emph{droṇī}, \textquotedblleft{}wooden trough\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 6641), through Prakrit \emph{dōṇī}: a tadbhava. A hollowed log carried water and people alike. CDIAL suggests the sense \textquotedblleft{}boat\textquotedblright{} may have mixed with a separate non-Aryan word, \emph{*ḍōṅga}.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Kannada for a lotus, then the Kannada for wheat, then say \emph{dōṇi} again

\section[\texorpdfstring{\kn{ಕಣ್ಣೀರು} (kaṇṇīru)}{ಕಣ್ಣೀರು (kaṇṇīru)}]{\kn{ಕಣ್ಣೀರು} (kaṇṇīru) — tears}

\label{lesson:KA-C139-kanniru}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Kannada for wheat, then the Kannada for a boat.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಕಣ್ಣೀರು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಕಣ್ಣೀರು}} — \emph{kaṇṇīru} — \textquotedblleft{}tears\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಕಣ್ಣೀರು}} (\emph{kaṇṇīru}) is native Dravidian, \textquotedblleft{}eye-water\textquotedblright{}: \emph{kaṇ}, \textquotedblleft{}eye\textquotedblright{} (DEDR 1159), and \emph{nīru}, \textquotedblleft{}water\textquotedblright{} (DEDR 3690). DEDR 1159 lists the compound itself as Kannada \emph{kaṇ ṇīr}. DEDR 3690 compares Sanskrit \emph{nīra}.
\end{cousinweb}
